summary: The chart beat line does not advance within the measure in Simple half/whole note mode
detail: In Simple, practice.js's scheduleSimpleBeat only pushes to scheduledLog inside `if (chord && shouldTrigger)`, and shouldTrigger is `beatInMeasure % noteBeats === 0` - so with whole notes an entry is logged once a measure and with half notes every other beat. scheduledLog is what syncHighlight reads to write #measureReadout ("2.3"), and stage.js's beatLine() reads that to set --beat on the sounding bar, so the fill sits still between note attacks instead of sweeping a quarter per beat. The log is described in its own comment as being for syncing the visual highlight, so the fix is probably to log every beat whether or not a note sounds, keeping the note-firing inside the trigger test - check the styled path around line 935 doesn't have the same gap. Reported 2026-09-08; not started.
resolution: Done 2026-09-08. scheduleSimpleBeat pushed to scheduledLog inside `if (chord && shouldTrigger)`, so on half notes it logged every other beat and on whole notes one beat a measure. That log is the chart's clock - syncHighlight reads it to write #measureReadout, and stage.js reads that to set --beat - so the line sat still between attacks. The push now happens every beat, outside the trigger test; only the note-firing stays inside. The styled path already logged every beat, so it needed nothing. Measured through the readout, with requestAnimationFrame redirected onto a timer because the test browser freezes it: on Simple whole note it went 1.1, 2.1, 1.1, 2.1 before and 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 2.4 after; half note and quarter note both walk all four beats too. No test - the suite can't drive the scheduler, since a suspended AudioContext's currentTime never advances. Tests 293/293.

summary: The genre player queues notes into the past after a stall, the same way the practice tab did
detail: genre-examples.js schedules with the same shape the practice tab had before T35's neighbour was fixed: LOOKAHEAD_MS 25, SCHEDULE_AHEAD 0.15, and a `while (startTime + nextSlot * secondsPerSlot < now + SCHEDULE_AHEAD)` loop that catches up by scheduling every missed slot at a time that has already passed. A throttled timer in an unfocused tab therefore fires a pile of note attacks on one instant - popping - just as it did in CAGED practice at funk/180. The fix there was to widen the cushion to 0.4s, step over slots whose moment has gone, and call off the queue on stop via GT.audio.cancelScheduled(), which already exists and is not tab-specific. Same treatment should work here; mind that this player loops and has its own stopTimer. Noticed 2026-09-08 while fixing the practice tab; not started.
resolution: Done 2026-09-08. Same three moves as the practice tab, sharing its code rather than repeating it: the counting helper moved into audio.js as stepsToSkip(cursor, now, step) and both players call it, cancelScheduled() was already there and is now called from the genre player's stop() too, and SCHEDULE_AHEAD went 0.15 -> 0.4. One case is the genre player's own: a stall can carry the cursor past the end of a run that isn't looping, so the scheduler now ends the run there instead of wrapping round and replaying it. Measured on skate punk at 190: 1s and 2.5s stalls put nothing in the past (worst leads +17ms and +82ms), steady-state minimum lead 372ms; stopping mid-run called off all 16 queued notes with none leaking; a 6s stall during a non-looping run ended it cleanly rather than looping.

summary: The first Dsus4 shown drops the 5th, so it reads as a bare fourth
detail: Noticed 2026-09-08 while checking fingerings. The sus4 formula marks only [0,5] as essential, so findChordVoicings ranks x-x-0-0-3-3 (D, G and nothing else) above the everyday x-x-0-2-3-3 (D, G, A). D and G alone aren't really a sus chord - they're a bare fourth, and could as easily read as G. The canonical shape is still shown, just not first, so CANON_PRESENT passes. Either the 5th should be essential for sus chords, or the ranking should prefer a voicing carrying all three tones. Check the other sus/power formulas for the same before changing anything.
resolution: Done 2026-09-08. The sus2 and sus4 formulas now carry the 5th in their essential list. A triad can drop its 5th and still be itself, which is what the essential lists are for, but a sus chord can't: the sus note is heard against the 5th, and root plus 4th is a bare fourth. The app's own reverse finder agrees - it calls D and G "G5" before "Dsus4". After the change no sus chord has a single fifth-less shape (Dsus4 had 6 of 20, Esus4 4 of 18, Gsus4 4, Asus2 3, Csus2 1), the everyday x-x-0-2-3-3 reads first, and the totals barely move because the finder fills the freed places with real voicings. Dsus4 was promoted from CANON_PRESENT to CANON so the shape is held to reading first, and a new test asserts no sus chord is ever offered without its 5th. Both fail on the old code with the reported symptom. Tests 294/294.

summary: stringSetTriads carries three guard clauses that never fire
detail: Found 2026-09-08 while writing the close-triad golden master: perturbing the rising-pitch check, the one-of-each-tone check and maxSpan each changed the output not at all, because the close-voicing rule (under an octave) plus the per-string chord-tone filter already imply all three. Adjacent strings are 4-5 semitones apart, so within an octave three rising chord tones can't repeat a tone or span more than four frets. The code isn't wrong - it's over-specified, which makes it read as though those rules are doing work. Worth either removing them with a comment saying why they're unnecessary, or keeping them and saying they're belt-and-braces. The golden master now pins the output either way.
resolution: Done 2026-09-08 - by measuring it properly and writing down what's true, not by deleting anything. The first claim was wrong: probing the four rules one at a time made three look dead, because each is covered by the others. Testing them in combination over 288 root/quality/string-set cases (850 voicings) shows the minimal pair is close-voicing plus rising - those two alone reproduce the output exactly, while dropping either changes it. The other two, one-of-each-tone and the hand span, are implied by that pair: three rising chord tones inside an octave can't repeat a tone or spread beyond a hand, given adjacent strings four or five semitones apart. Kept rather than removed - each names something a player would say about a close triad, maxSpan is a parameter a caller could still pass (none does today), and the golden master holds the output either way. The function's comment now says which two are load-bearing so the next reader doesn't spend the time I did.

summary: Em is fingered index-and-middle where it is usually taught middle-and-ring
detail: Checked against sources 2026-09-08. computeFingering puts the index on the A string and the middle on the D for the open Em (0-2-2-0-0-0), because its rule is that the lowest fret takes the lowest finger and Em has only one fret in play. Fender and most teaching use middle and ring, which keeps the index free and makes the fingers identical to E major minus the index, so E-Em switching costs nothing; til.co lists ours as the alternative, so it isn't wrong, just not the convention. Every other common chord checked matches the sources exactly (G 2-1-0-0-0-3, A 1-2-3, the B barre 1-2-3-4-1, F 1-3-4-2-1-1, the open sevenths). A fix would need a rule that doesn't disturb those - the current fingering is pinned by FINGERINGS, so any change will show itself.
resolution: Done 2026-09-08. Em is now middle-and-ring. The reason it can't come out of the rule is Asus2: the same shape (two notes, one fret, adjacent strings) is conventionally index-and-middle, because Asus2 is A major with the ring lifted while Em is E major with the index lifted. Sources agree on both. So the fix is a table, CONVENTIONAL_FINGERING in chord-finder.js, consulted before the rule and holding the one shape whose convention the geometry can't give - the same move CAGED_DUP_ROOT_STRING and SCALE_SHAPES make. The verification pass covered C, Am, Dm, G, A, E, Em, Asus2, F, B, B7 against til.co, Fender, guitarchordslibrary and onlineguitarbooks; every one but Em already matched, and Asus2, Am, E, G and Em7 are unchanged by the fix. One caution recorded: a web-search summary garbled the F barre, putting fret numbers where the finger numbers belonged - fetching the page itself gave ring on the A string, little on the D, middle on the G, which is what the app already had. Tests 293/293.

summary: Hide the neck controls automatically on a phone held in landscape
detail: Asked for 2026-09-08. A phone turned sideways is the case where the neck wants the whole screen and the controls are in the way, and it's also the case where the Controls button has to be found and pressed first. See whether the controls can default to hidden there without touching desktop or tablet. body.controls-off already does the hiding; what's needed is a way to detect the case. A width breakpoint alone won't do it - a landscape phone is about as wide as a portrait tablet. Candidates worth trying: (orientation: landscape) combined with a short max-height (a phone in landscape is roughly 320-450px tall, a tablet 700+), (hover: none) and (pointer: coarse) to rule out desktop, and matchMedia in stage.js rather than CSS since setControls is JS state and the Controls button has to stay in step with it. Mind that the current setControls(window.innerWidth >= 700) runs once at load - it would need to follow a rotation, and it must not override a choice already made by hand. INVESTIGATED 2026-09-08. Detection: solved and exact. `(orientation: landscape) and (max-height: 500px) and (pointer: coarse)` picks out a landscape phone and nothing else - measured at 375x812 portrait phone (no, and already hidden by the width rule), 844x390 landscape phone (yes), 768x1024 iPad portrait (no, wrong orientation), 1024x768 iPad landscape (no, 768 is taller than 500), and a 1200x480 desktop window (landscape and short - excluded only by pointer). The pointer clause is the load-bearing one: it is the sole thing separating a landscape phone from a short desktop window. Must be matchMedia in stage.js rather than CSS, because setControls also writes aria-pressed on the Controls button and CSS alone would make that button lie; and it needs a listener for rotation plus a flag so it stops overriding once the button has been pressed by hand. But the premise doesn't hold. At 844x390 the page is 743px tall against a 390px viewport - 353px over - and hiding the controls frees only 133 of that, leaving 220. The neck is off screen either way. The chart is what takes the room: 246px of it, being six bars in two rows of large serif type. Simulated a landscape layout by injecting CSS - site header hidden, chart as one row of six at 20px, tighter padding, controls off - and the document came to 408px with the neck fully visible above the transport (top 126, bottom 287, transport at 311). So the thing asked for is reachable, but it is a landscape layout rather than a toggle: hiding the controls on its own does not put the neck on screen. Needs a decision on how much of the chart and header to give up in landscape before anything is built.
resolution: Done 2026-09-10. Three parts. The detection is a matchMedia in stage.js for (orientation: landscape) and (max-height: 500px) and (pointer: coarse) - height tells a phone from a tablet, pointer tells it from a short desktop window - with a rotation listener and a flag so pressing the Controls button stops the default overruling you. The chart shrinks in landscape: names at clamp(15px, 3vw, 21px), tighter padding, and the key and progression back on one line rather than stacked the way an upright phone stacks them. And the transport folds to a floating Play from a chevron at its right end, which frees the ~80px it was using. Measured at 667x375, an iPhone SE sideways: the page was 533px against a 375px viewport before, and with the smaller chart and the bar folded it is 388 with the neck fully on screen (187-321). Unchanged at 375x812, 768x1024, 1024x768 and 1400x900 - the chord names still measure 30, 32, 43 and 44px there. The collapse button is hidden on an upright phone, where it had nowhere to go: it was overlapping the tempo readout. One thing the landscape rules needed twice: they have to sit after the max-width:760px phone block in the stylesheet, or at 667px wide both match and the phone block wins on order. Tests 294/294.

summary: Let the chord picker reach non-diatonic roots, keeping the degrees clearly marked
detail: Asked for 2026-09-10. Today each slot's first picker offers only the seven degrees of the key (plus the harmonic-minor V in minor), so a chord whose root isn't in the key can't be chosen at all - a bVII in major, a bVI, a tritone sub - even though the second picker will already put any quality on a degree. Widen the root list to all twelve, but don't flatten the distinction: a root the key owns should still read as its degree (`Dm - ii`), and one it doesn't should read as what it is (`Bb` or `bVII`) so it's plain you've stepped outside. Things to work through: the slot stores a degree (slotChoices) and chordForDegree builds from it, so a non-diatonic root needs somewhere to live in that model - probably a pitch class rather than a degree, with the numeral worked out from the interval above the tonic; transposing on a key change should move it by the same interval (loadProgression already does that for genre-example chords, so there's a pattern to follow); the numeral has to stay right in both modes; and shareState writes `c` as degree.bars.shape, which won't hold a root that isn't a degree - the `n` (chord names) form it already uses for genre progressions may be the answer.
resolution: Done 2026-09-10. The root picker now offers all twelve in two groups: "In this key" holds the degrees exactly as before (Dm - ii, plus the harmonic-minor V in minor), and "Outside the key" holds the five the key has no chord for (Bb - bVII). A borrowed root lives in the same slot the degree does, written 'c' plus the semitones above the tonic ('c10' is a bVII), so it is stored relative to the key the way a degree is - which is what makes it survive everything a degree survives with no new machinery: transposing moves it by the same interval, and shareState's degree.bars.shape needs no new format because 'c10' is just another root token. chordForDegree now starts from a new baseChordFor(), which returns the key's own chord for a degree and a plain major triad for a borrowed root; every other helper (the diatonic seventh, the shape list, the quality picker) goes through it, so the two kinds of root differ in one place rather than in nine. Numerals needed no work at all - DEGREE_NUMERALS already covered all twelve semitones in both modes. Spelling did: NOTE_NAMES_SHARP would have made a bVII read A#, so theory.js gains NOTE_NAMES_FLAT and the root is spelled from the accidental in its own numeral. Two things worth recording. A mode change can make a borrowed root diatonic - the bIII of C major is the III of C minor - so transposeToKey hands it back to that degree; without that the chord still sounds right but loses its pin, and the next share link falls back to the chord-names form. And the shape list for a borrowed root cannot be Object.keys(CHORD_SHAPES): '7' is number-like, so JS enumerates it first and the menu opened on 7 instead of Major. Both are covered by tests, checked to fail when the code is broken. Tests 296/296.

summary: Ear training modes for pentatonics and scales
detail: Asked for 2026-09-10, straight after the chord drill landed. Today the tab drills one chord shape: notesOf() reduces a voicing's cells to one answer per pitch class, and the answers are the chord's own tones with their degrees. A scale or pentatonic mode needs three things it hasn't got. The notes come from somewhere else - SCALE_BOXES and PENTA_BOXES in fretboard.js, keyed by mode and box rather than by chord formula - so the source of "the notes on show" wants to be a parameter rather than a voicing. The picture is different too: a scale box is a stretch of the whole neck, which neck.js draws for the practice tab, not a chord diagram, so the shape card and the shape picker sheet would both need a second kind of drawing (and the note-name/degree labels beside the strings only exist in the chord diagram). And the question changes: over seven notes, "which degree was that" is the useful drill rather than "which of these four", and the answer buttons would want the scale degrees (1-7, or with the mode's accidentals) rather than chord tones. Worth deciding whether the answer is by degree, by note name, or both, and whether the root drone should sound under it - hearing a 6th against a root is a different exercise from hearing it cold. The existing pieces that carry over: the drill loop (ask, answer, verdict, auto-play the next), the piano voice, and playOne(string, fret).
resolution: Done 2026-09-10. A Drill picker at the top of the tab: Chord, Pentatonic, Scale. The pentatonic and scale modes take a key and a scale (the two pentatonics; the seven modes) and draw the CAGED box across the whole neck with neck.js, degree labels on every note and the roots ringed - the same written-out boxes the practice tab draws, from pentaBoxPlacements and scaleBoxPlacements. Answering by degree rather than by note turned out to be a false choice: the buttons carry both, exactly as the chord mode's do, so it reads 'E flat / b3' and you can use whichever you think in. Scale degrees count from 1 where a chord's count from its root, so the 2nd of a scale is a 2 and not the 9th it would be over a chord - a separate table. No root drone in the end; the Play root button covers it and is one press. The three modes share everything below the picture, because describe() returns the same shape of thing for all of them - cells, root, notes, names - and nothing past it asks which mode is on. The clickable notes needed the finder's note machinery split in two: notesOnClick lights and sounds single notes in any container, soundOnClick adds the whole-shape tour on top for a chord card. One click path per container, or a note sounds twice for one press. Also asked for and done: a Play setting to narrow a box to one octave or leave it whole. Which octave took measuring - usually the one above the box's lowest root, but a box clipped by the nut can have its lowest root so high the octave above it runs off the top of the shape. Swept all 582 boxes across every scale and root: three have a higher root whose octave holds more, and A major pentatonic's A box is 3 notes above the lowest root against 5 above the next. So the fullest octave wins, and the test walks all twelve roots because two wouldn't meet one of the three. Tests 326/326, both new ones checked to fail when their invariant is broken.

summary: Look for free-to-use recordings of real guitar notes for the chords and the ear drills
detail: Asked for 2026-09-10. Everything is synthesized today: the chord finder, the reverse finder and the ear trainer all sound notes through audio.js's piano voice (playNote), and the genre examples through a detuned-sawtooth guitar. Real recorded notes would sound like a guitar in a way a synthesized one can't, and it matters most in the ear trainer, where the whole exercise is hearing what a note is. What's wanted: one sample per note over the range the app draws (open E at 82Hz up to the 15th fret on the high e, around 880Hz) - or a few per octave, pitch-shifted between, which is how a sampler does it. THE LICENCE IS THE JOB, not an afterthought: be very sure the recordings are actually free to use for this, including redistribution in a public repo, and read the actual licence rather than a summary or a search result - freesound.org and the like carry CC0, CC-BY and non-commercial side by side under the same search, and a CC-BY sample needs its attribution shipped. Whatever is chosen, put a comment in the code saying where the files came from, which licence they're under, and why we believe that licence permits this use, with a link - so the next reader can check the reasoning rather than trusting it. Also worth weighing before committing to it: the app is dependency-free and opens from file://, so samples mean either a pile of audio files beside the HTML or base64 inside it, and either way the page stops being one file you can email to someone. A hybrid - synthesized by default, samples if they're present - may be the honest answer.
resolution: Done 2026-09-10. The recordings are fifteen notes of a 2017 Martin HD-28 Vintage Series, one every two or three semitones from E2 to B5, recorded and mapped by Jeff Learman for Kinwie's Discord SFZ GM bank and taken from the sfzinstruments fork of it. They cover the app's whole range (MIDI 40-79) with nothing stretched more than three semitones, and they are CC0. On the licence, which was the job: the terms are stated by the author himself in the header of the .sfz that maps these very samples, identically in the upstream repo and the fork, repeated in a second .sfz beside them, under a bank whose README says each instrument is licensed by its creator and only CC0, CC-BY and equivalents are allowed. CC0 asks nothing, not even attribution; we credit him anyway. Two libraries were rejected and the reasons are written down so nobody re-checks them: the Philharmonia's samples may be used in a finished work but 'must not be sold or made available as is', which is exactly what committing them to a public repo would be; and VCSL is genuinely CC0 but has no guitar - its composite chordophones are two harps and a strumstick. The reasoning lives in audio/guitar/SOURCE.md and, in full, in a comment over the sample table in audio.js. On the file:// question raised while doing this: a pile of files beside the page is fine, but only over http. Firefox and Chrome both give a file:// page an opaque origin since CVE-2019-11730, so it cannot fetch its own neighbours, and Web Audio needs an ArrayBuffer to decode. So the samples are a bonus: each is fetched the first time a note needs it (~30ms local, nothing after), and any failure sets a flag that falls the whole app back to the synthesized piano silently and for good. Proved both ways by counting what the audio graph builds - with the fetch working, one buffer source and no oscillators; with it stubbed to reject, two oscillators and the piano's hammer, no unhandled rejections. The three sound entry points in chord-finder.js are async now: they wake the audio inside the click (a context first resumed after an await may be refused), then await the samples, then schedule. The practice tab is untouched and stays a piano. 3.0MB of wav in the repo, kept as wav rather than transcoded so there's no codec question and no quality call I can't hear. Tests 324/324.

summary: Keep score for the session: right answers, tries, and percent
detail: Asked for 2026-09-10. The drill says whether each answer was right and then moves on, so nothing accumulates - there's no way to tell a good run from a bad one, or to see yourself improve over a sitting. Wanted: right answers, total tries, and the percentage, for the current session. Points to settle when building it. What counts as a try - every button press, or one per question (so three wrong guesses on one note is one question got wrong)? Percent correct means different things under each, and the second is the more honest measure of hearing. When does the count reset - a new chord, a new shape, or only a page load? Rolling a chord mid-run and keeping the score is probably right, since the drill is the same drill. Where it goes: the verdict line already sits under the answers and is the natural home, but it's an aria-live region that reads out on every change, so a score parked in it would be announced each time - it likely wants its own element. The state is three numbers next to `asked` in ear-training.js; the awkward part is only the question of what a try is.
resolution: Done 2026-09-10, alongside T42. Right answers, questions asked and the percentage, in the quiz head opposite the question. The two things the row left open: a try is a question, not a button press - three wrong stabs at one note is one question missed, which is the honest measure of whether you heard it - and the count runs for as long as the tab is open, surviving a new chord, a new box and a change of drill, since it's the same drill and a run you can't interrupt isn't worth keeping. It has its own element rather than sharing the verdict line, which is an aria-live region that would otherwise read the score out after every answer.

summary: The octave stepper can reach a partial octave at the top of a box but not at the bottom
detail: Reported 2026-09-10. In one-octave mode the up/down arrows walk the octaves a box holds, and at the top you can land on an incomplete one - the octave above the highest root runs off the end of the shape, and stepping to it is allowed. At the bottom you can't: the notes below the lowest root belong to no octave at all and can never be selected. It should be symmetrical. The cause is in octavesOf() in ear-training.js: it takes each root in turn and collects the cells from that root up to twelve semitones above it, so every octave it offers begins on a root and nothing is ever built downward to one. What's missing is an octave that ENDS on the lowest root - the cells from lowestRoot minus 12 up to lowestRoot - offered only when the box actually holds notes down there, and prepended so the arrows reach it below the current first. Three things to mind while doing it. fullestOctave() picks the default by how many of the scale's notes an octave holds; a partial bottom octave must not become the default just because of how the counting falls, so the default probably wants to be chosen among the complete ones first. The test testOneOctaveOfABox in tests.js asserts that the octave starts on a root of the box, which a bottom octave doesn't - it ends on one - so that assertion becomes 'starts or ends on a root'. And the up/down arrows disable at the ends by comparing octaveIdx against subject.octaves, which stays right as long as the new octave is added to the same list rather than special-cased.
resolution: Done 2026-09-10. octavesOf() now offers a tail built downward to the lowest root - the cells from twelve semitones below it up to it - added only when the box actually holds notes down there, and put at the front so the arrows reach it below what used to be the first octave. In C major's C box that's the octave 40-48, six of the seven notes; the E box has nothing below its lowest root and still offers two octaves rather than a phantom third. The default had to learn a tiebreak: fullestOctave() still takes the octave holding most of the scale, but where two hold as many it now prefers the one that begins on a root, because the tail is somewhere to step to rather than somewhere to start. C major's D box is exactly that case - the tail 50-60 holds all seven notes, as does 60-72, and the one starting on the root is the right default. The test's 'starts on a root' became 'has a root at one end', and it works out the candidate spans itself - up from each root, and down to the lowest - rather than asking the module, so the two can still disagree. Tests 326/326.

summary: Put the state in the URL so any exercise in any tool can be bookmarked
detail: Asked for 2026-09-10. The URL carries the tab today - tabs.js keeps a slug like #chord-finder - and the practice tab alone carries its progression after a question mark (#caged-practice?k=major:C&c=0.2.,4.2.&t=120), which shareState/applyShareState in practice.js write and read. Nothing else does, so a chord finder search, an ear-training drill or a genre example can't be bookmarked or sent to anyone. Wanted: the same treatment for every tool. The pieces are mostly there. tabs.js already parses the fragment into slug + query and exposes stateParams(); what's missing is a way for a tab to WRITE its state back without fighting the tab slug, since writeHash() only ever writes the slug. So the first job is a small shared thing in tabs.js - something like GT.tabs.setState(name, params) that rewrites the fragment as slug?query, with replaceState rather than pushState so that twiddling a control doesn't fill the back button with fifty entries. Then each tab needs a read and a write: the chord finder wants the chord name plus its shapes/dots-show/shell toggles; the reverse finder the notes picked; the ear trainer the drill, the chord or key and scale, the shape, the octave, whether root-first is on, and which qualities are enabled; the genre examples the style and the pattern. Two things to decide before writing any of it. Whether a rolled question should be in the URL at all - bookmarking 'A minor pentatonic, G shape, one octave' is clearly useful, but pinning the exact note being asked is probably not, and the ear trainer would want to roll a fresh question on load. And whether writing state on every control change is right, or only on an explicit share - the practice tab has a copy-link button and writes the fragment when you press it, which is quieter and might be the pattern to follow everywhere.
resolution: Done 2026-09-10. tabs.js gained setState(name, params): it rewrites the fragment as slug?query, refuses to write for a tab that isn't the one on show, and uses replaceState - a control you twiddled is not a place you navigated to, and forty of them would leave the back button useless. Reading was already there in stateParams(). Four tabs now write and read their own: the chord finder (the chord typed plus the shapes/dots/shell/triad toggles), the reverse finder (the notes picked, written the way this app writes a grip everywhere else - n=x-x-5-6-7-7), the ear trainer (the drill, the chord or the key and scale, the shape, the octave, root-first, and which qualities are on) and the genre examples (style, rhythm or lead, pattern, progression). Both decisions the row left open went the same way. The question a drill happens to be asking is NOT in the URL - a bookmark should reopen the exercise, not one moment of it, and Random is right there for wanting another. And state is written continuously rather than behind a share button, because bookmarking is the ask and a browser bookmarks what's in the address bar. The practice tab keeps its explicit copy-link: its state is a whole progression, it already had a share flow, and rewriting twelve chords into the URL on every twiddle would be noise. Order matters in tabs.js and it already worked out: show() writes the slug before calling onShow, but writeHash returns early when the slug is already right, so a link's query survives the load and a tab switch drops it - which is what you want either way. A round-trip test lives in tests-ear.js; the first version of it passed with the key deliberately left out of the URL, because the detour between writing and reading hadn't disturbed the state being restored. It disturbs it properly now and fails as it should. Tests 331/331.

summary: A detailed UX review of the ear trainer, with options
detail: Asked for 2026-09-10, once the fourth drill and the URL state had landed. The tab has grown quickly - four drills, a mode picker, a chord field or a key-and-scale pair, a Random button, a shape stepper and a shape sheet, an octave setting with its own arrows, a quality switch board of nineteen, four play buttons, a root-first toggle, a Back button, a score and a verdict line - and nothing has been stood back from and looked at as a whole. Wanted: a proper review of the thing as a piece of design, with options rather than one answer, so the choosing stays with me. Worth covering: how many controls are on screen before you've answered anything and which of them could wait until they're wanted; whether the four drills belong behind one picker at all or whether the quality drill is a different exercise wearing the same clothes; the vertical order - the picture is above the question, so on a phone the answers can be below the fold; what a first-time visitor sees, since the tab opens on a random chord with no explanation of what it wants; whether the score should be more present, or a streak, or nothing; and what happens after a run - there's no notion of finishing, only of continuing. Look at the phone layout specifically: it was never designed for, only inherited. Screenshots or mockups of the options would help more than prose.
resolution: Done 2026-09-10. Written up as an artifact rather than prose, since the row asked for mockups: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/d59b6946-b49b-4338-a444-ecf0ece9552a - nine findings, four of them measured off the running tab, three options drawn at phone width against the current layout, and a recommendation. The measurements are the part worth keeping here in case the artifact goes missing. On a 375x667 phone in the Chord drill the answer buttons begin at y=702 in a 667-tall viewport, so you cannot see the question and the answers at once and every question costs a scroll each way. The neck starts at y=239 - 36% of the screen is setup before anything you came for. Visible controls by drill: chord 19, pentatonic 24, scale 26, quality 33, the last because all nineteen quality switches are permanently on screen. And the neck draws fifteen frets for a box that uses four or five. The options: A, question first (setup collapses to one line, the neck moves below the answers) - cheap, risks nothing, and it's the one recommended; B, hide the neck while answering and reveal it with the note lit - a purer ear exercise but a worse study aid, recommended as a switch on top of A if at all; C, runs of ten with a start and a result, which also gives the tab somewhere to say what it wants from a first-time visitor. Plus five that fit any of them: make the question button primary, draw only the frets the box uses (the chord finder's diagram already does), collapse the quality switches behind a summary, grid the answers instead of wrapping them four-and-one, and give the quality drill its own tab since it shares the drill loop and not the chrome. Nothing was built.

summary: Put everything the practice tab is showing in the URL, the fretboard view included
detail: Asked for 2026-09-10, right after T46 put the other four tabs' state in the address bar. The practice tab already carries half of it: shareState/applyShareState in practice.js write k (mode:tonic), c (the chords as degree.bars.shape), n (chord names for a loaded genre progression), l (its label), t (tempo) and s (style.variant). What's missing is everything the fretboard below it is doing, which lives in fretboard-view.js and is a good deal of state: the view (roots / chords / triads / pentatonic / scales), neck or position, which box you're on, which of the five CAGED shapes are enabled, the colour mode, follow-playback, the arpeggio setting, the label mode, and the scale-theory choice (modal or parallel). Right now none of it survives a link, so a shared progression arrives with the neck showing whatever the recipient last had. Two things to settle. The practice tab was deliberately left writing its state only when you press Copy link (T46), on the grounds that its state is large and it already had a share flow - this row is the case for changing that, so decide whether it now writes continuously like the others (consistent, bookmarkable by the browser's own button) or keeps the explicit press (quieter, and the URL stays legible). And the fragment is already long; adding a dozen view fields will make it longer, so it's worth deciding whether the defaults are omitted (they are today, for tempo and style) and whether the view state deserves short keys or one packed field.
resolution: Done 2026-09-10. Both halves of the row settled. The tab now writes its state continuously, like the other four, rather than only when Copy link is pressed: the view state it carries is exactly what a bookmark should hold - which box of which shape, coloured how - and a setting you must remember to press a button to keep is a setting you lose. Copy link stays, since putting the address on the clipboard is what the address bar can't do for itself. The fretboard travels as ONE field, f, rather than a dozen parameters: a letter, a colon, a value, joined by dots, and anything sitting at its default is left out, so a neck at rest adds nothing at all. It carries the view mode, neck-or-position, the box number, which CAGED shapes are on (as the letters themselves), the colour mode, follow-playback, the arpeggio toggle, the fret range, the position method, the string set and the scale theory. Restoring works by pressing the controls rather than assigning to the variables behind them - every one of those settings has a handler that re-bases the box, greys out what no longer applies and redraws, and pressing the control runs all of it the way a hand would; the box number is the exception, since it has only arrows. applyViewState sets every field, not just the ones the link mentions, so a link lands the same way on a fresh page as on one somebody has been playing with. fretboard-view tells its host when it has redrawn (host.viewChanged) and the practice tab writes the address then; a redraw that changes nothing the link carries writes nothing, because the address is compared before it is replaced. Host callbacks now default, so a host written before a hook existed keeps working - which is what the fretboard tests are. Test: the defaults write nothing, a state round-trips through the controls, and a string naming one field still puts the others back to their defaults; sabotaged that last rule and watched it fail.

summary: Free-to-use samples for the practice tab too
detail: Asked for 2026-09-10, after T43 put a real recorded guitar in the two finders and the ear trainer. The practice tab still plays everything synthesized: playNote's piano for the chords, playBass for the bass, and the genre voices (a detuned-sawtooth guitar, the drum recipes) for the styles. What T43 leaves in place to build on: audio/guitar/ holds fifteen CC0 notes of a Martin HD-28, audio.js has playPluck/readyForPluck/pluckReady and a fetch-on-demand cache that falls back to the synth silently, and audio/guitar/SOURCE.md records the licence reasoning and the two libraries already rejected. So a guitar-voiced progression is mostly a matter of routing the practice tab's chord playback through playPluck. The harder parts are the ones T43 didn't have to touch. The practice tab plays a chord on a beat, in time, with a scheduler that queues 0.4s ahead - so samples have to be resident before the beat rather than fetched at it, which means warming the whole set when playback starts rather than one note at a time. A piano is arguably the right voice for a progression anyway, since it stays out of the way of the guitar you are playing over it - worth deciding whether this is a choice (a voice picker: piano or guitar) rather than a replacement. And the styles want more than single notes: a strummed pattern, a palm-muted chug and a walking bass are different articulations, not one sample pitched about, so either the style voices stay synthesized or the search starts again for a library that covers them - and the licence has to be checked as carefully as it was in T43, with the reasoning written into the code beside the files.
resolution: Done 2026-09-10. Searched again for a free-to-use library covering the practice tab's other voices and came back with nothing usable, so the tab got a Voice choice over the recordings T43 already brought in rather than a new download. What was looked at: the Discord SFZ GM bank, whose nylon guitar, muted guitar and acoustic bass turn out to be //dummy stubs with no audio behind them - only 034-Electric Bass (finger) is real, and although its header says CC0 ("From Killer Bass by Karyrofer (http://karoryfer.com) / License: CC0") the karoryfer.com URL now 302s to a shop, so the licence can't be verified where it was granted; at 45 files and 21.5 MB, taken on a broken link, for a bass line, it wasn't worth it. Same standard as T43: if the grant can't be read at the source, we don't ship the files. What was built instead: a Piano/Guitar segmented control in the practice tab's Set up sheet routing playChord through the CC0 Martin HD-28 samples, strummed 16 ms apart rather than struck together; warmGuitar() fetches the whole set on Play, since the scheduler queues 0.4s ahead and a chord can't wait for a download; any chord whose notes aren't resident falls to the piano per chord, which is what a file:// page gets permanently; v=guitar rides in the share link. Measured in the browser: with the guitar chosen, a chord builds three buffer sources and no oscillators, and before the samples arrive the same click builds six oscillators - the fallback proven rather than assumed. A new invariant walks all 144 root/quality combinations through chordFromName and chordFrequencies and fails if any note falls outside the sample map or more than three semitones from a sample. The bass and the genre styles stay synthesized: a strum, a palm-muted chug and a walking bass are different articulations, not one note pitched about.

summary: Type a progression in as chord names instead of picking each chord through the menus
detail: Asked for 2026-09-10. The practice tab's chords are set one at a time through the Set up sheet: a degree picker, a bar count and a shape picker per slot, plus the preset list and the dice. That is good for rolling something at random and slow for entering a progression you already know. Wanted: a text field you can type "E E E E A7 A7 E E Bm7 Bm7" into, one bar per token, so a repeated chord is just repeated. The pieces to build on are all there - chordFromName/parseChordName in theory.js already read names like E, A7 and Bm7, the share link's n= field already carries a progression as chord names for genre examples (practice.js shareState), and applyShareState already turns names back into slots. Things to settle: whether typed chords set the key or are read against whichever key is set (a typed Bm7 in E major is a numeral the roller would never pick, which is part of the point), what to do with a name that doesn't parse (refuse the whole line, or mark the token), whether the typed text is the source of truth or is parsed into the existing per-slot state and then forgotten, and whether the field replaces the per-chord pickers or sits beside them as a second way in.
resolution: Done 2026-09-10. A "Type it" field in the Set up sheet's Progression section, with a Set button and Enter to apply. One token a bar, so "E E E E A7 A7 E E Bm7 Bm7" is four chords held for four, two, two and two - runs collapse through loadProgression, the same road a genre example takes in. Tokens split on whitespace, commas and bar lines, because people write "A | D | E" and "C, Am, F, G". Decisions the row asked for: the key follows the chords (first chord is the tonic, its quality picks the mode) rather than the chords being read against the current key - half the point of typing is to reach what the dice can't, and reading against the key would throw that away; a word it can't read refuses the whole line and names the word, since a progression with a hole in it isn't what anyone meant; too many chord changes is refused rather than truncated; and the field is a view of the state rather than the state itself - it reads back whatever is set, so it doubles as a plain-text view of the chart, and it stops rewriting itself while you're typing in it. Test drives all of it, including bar lines, the refusal, and that the chart is left alone when a line is refused.

summary: An upbeat blues style with straight eighths rather than a shuffle
detail: Asked for 2026-09-10. The Blues style in audio.js STYLES has three variants today - Shuffle (a straight-shuffle boogie on the 1st and 3rd triplet of each beat), Slow blues (a sparse 12/8 ballad, just the turnaround bass and a held chord) and Train beat (a busy blues-rock shuffle) - and all three are swung, because all three are built on triplets. Wanted: a fourth that is straight-eighths and quicker in feel, the up-tempo jump/rock-and-roll blues rather than the shuffle - think a straight-eighth boogie or a Chuck Berry two-beat, where the eighths are even and the drive comes from the bass line and the backbeat rather than from the swing. The pieces are all there: a variant is a grid, a kick/snare/hat pattern, a chord rhythm and a bass line with per-slot offsets, so this is a new entry in the blues variants list plus a name. Worth deciding whether the bass walks the 1-3-5-6 boogie figure (which the Shuffle variant's bass offsets already know how to express) and what tempo the style's default should be, since the point of it is that it is faster than the ones already there.
resolution: Done 2026-09-10. Added as the Blues style's fourth variant, "Jump blues": a 16-slot grid so an eighth is two slots and the eighths land square, where the other three are built on triplets and therefore all shuffle. Kick on 0/6/8/14, a hard backbeat on 4 and 12 at 0.9 - the drive is meant to come from the backbeat and the bass rather than from a lilt - eighth-note hats throughout, and the boogie figure straight rather than swung: 1 3 5 6 b7 6 5 3, two slots a note. The comp started at six hits a bar and was cut to two after a listen: a jump band doesn't comp through this, the bass boogie is the engine and the horns punch 2 and 4, and six hits left no room to hear either. It is now the sparsest of the four blues variants (two chord hits a bar against Shuffle's five and Train beat's four). Dominant 7ths like the rest of the blues styles.

summary: An option to name the exact note, not just the pitch class, in the chord, pentatonic and scale drills
detail: Asked for 2026-09-11. The three note-finding drills ask which note is lit and accept the right pitch class: if a chord has two 5ths in it, either one answers. Wanted: a setting that makes you pick the one that actually sounded - the 5th on the D string at the 7th fret, not the 5th an octave up. The pieces: describe(i) in ear-training.js already knows the exact cell (string and fret) it chose, and choicesOf(s) builds the answer buttons from the shape's notes by degree, which is where the collapsing happens; twinsOf already knows how to pair cells that share a name, since it was written to stop a wrong dot lighting up. Things to settle: what the buttons say when two of them would read "5" (string name, octave number, or a small neck diagram on the button), whether the option is per-drill or one setting for all three, and whether a near-miss - the right degree in the wrong octave - should be told apart from a plain wrong answer, since it is a different mistake.
resolution: Done 2026-09-11. An Answer setting in the ear trainer's setup - "Which note" (as before) or "Which one exactly" - applying to the chord, pentatonic and scale drills and hidden in the quality drill, where it means nothing. Turned on, choicesOf builds one button per cell rather than one per pitch class, keyed by string:fret and sorted low to high. The questions the row asked: the buttons carry the octave, and the string as well when two cells are the same pitch played in two places, which is the shortest thing that tells them apart; it is one setting for all three drills rather than one each; and a near miss is told apart from a wrong answer - pressing the right note in the wrong place marks the button 'close' in amber and says "that's the 5, but not that one", since it is a different mistake and the one the setting exists to train. It still costs the question. Also taught ask() the same trick it already knew for octaves: with Root first on, a question isn't set on the very cell the reference just played. Rides in the URL as x=1. Measured in the app: a whole C major scale box offers 7 buttons naming the note and 17 naming the exact one. Followed up the same day with a second answering design: "Point to it", where the answer is given by clicking the dot on the neck rather than reading a list of buttons. Asked whether that belongs in both answer modes and decided no - pointing is an exact answer by nature, since you cannot point vaguely at a C, and accepting a different C than the one pointed at would contradict the gesture; wanting "any C" is what the naming mode is for. So the Answer row is now three coherent questions rather than two settings crossed: Name the note (buttons, pitch class), Name the exact one (buttons, place), Point to it (neck, place). Pointing needed one rule the buttons don't: while a question stands a dot answers instead of sounding, since clicking round a box until one matches is a way to get every question right without hearing anything; before the drill starts and after it ends the dots play as they always did. Measured in the app: with a question up, clicking a dot creates no audio at all and marks the dot; before starting, the same click sounds the note. Rides in the URL as x=n. Settled 2026-09-11: the two button modes are gone and pointing is the only way a note drill is answered, so there is no Answer setting at all - the buttons were a list of what the diagram above them was already showing. The quality drill keeps buttons, having no place to point at. One thing fell out of the removal: a box is drawn whole even when one octave of it is in play, so some dots on screen are not among the answers; clicking one is now a misclick that says "that one is outside the octave in play" rather than a wrong answer that costs the question. And the drill now reports which cell it asked about (GT.earTraining.askedAt) - not shown anywhere, since that would be the answer, but a test that wants to press a particular wrong dot on purpose was otherwise reduced to pressing everything and hoping, which made it pass and fail by luck about half the time.

summary: The run counter flashes 11/10 before the score appears
detail: Reported 2026-09-11: "the ear training quiz briefly shows 11/10 before showing your score". At the end of a run of ten the counter is advanced before the finish is noticed, so there is a frame or two where the tally reads one more than the run length. Look at advance()/tick()/finish() in ear-training.js: the fix is either to notice the end before the count moves, or to clamp what the run bar prints to the run length. Worth checking the same path doesn't also let an eleventh question be drawn and thrown away, which would be the same bug with a worse symptom.
resolution: Done 2026-09-11. drawProgress printed `runAsked + 1` - "the question you're on" - which after the tenth answer is 11, and it stayed on screen for the 1.3s pause before the result replaced it. Clamped to the run length, so the last answer reads 10 of 10 until the result appears. The run itself was never wrong: no eleventh question is drawn, which the existing run test already pinned. The test now reads the counter between the answer and the pause, which is the only moment the bug was visible; put the +1 back and watched it report "11 of 10".

summary: A mode that suggests a guitar part - rhythm and fills - to play over the progression
detail:
Asked for 2026-09-11. The practice tab plays a backing and leaves you to invent what goes over it. Wanted: a mode that suggests an actual part to play along with - a rhythm figure plus fills - one per style, so there is something concrete to try rather than a blank neck. Each part should combine a strumming or comping pattern with fills that fit the chord changes, in the idiom of the style it belongs to.

WHAT TO BUILD ON. Most of the machinery exists in the genre examples tab and is not tied to it: genre-data.js already holds rhythms (a grid, hits with mute/part flags, a voicing name and a tone) and leads (notes as string, fret, slot, duration) per genre; genres.js turns those into voiced cells with buildRhythm/buildLead and knows how to place a voicing for a named chord (voiceChord); tab.js draws the result as tablature with a playhead. So the work is less about inventing a format than about writing parts that follow a rolled progression in any key - the genre examples play fixed progressions, while this has to transpose to whatever the dice gave you - and about where the part is shown: tab under the chart, on the neck as shapes, or both.

THINGS TO SETTLE. Whether a part is picked per style/feel (so Jump blues has its own) or per progression; whether fills are placed by bar (a turnaround in the last bar, a pickup into the change) or offered as a vocabulary you choose from; whether it plays the part as well as showing it, which the genre tab already can; and how it reacts to a chord the part wasn't written for - a borrowed bVII, a typed Bm7 - since the progression can be anything.

IP. Design parts from the idiom rather than from recordings: the common rhythmic figures, the scale and arpeggio shapes, the turnarounds that belong to a style. Research is for what makes a style sound like itself - where the backbeat sits, which degrees the fills lean on, whether the part is chordal or single-note - not for transcribing anyone's playing. A specific recorded performance and a specific composition are both somebody's; a boogie figure or a minor-pentatonic turnaround is nobody's. Avoid signature riffs even where they are technically simple, since the point of a signature riff is that it is recognisable. Write down which sources informed each part and what was taken from them (style traits, not notes), the way audio/*/SOURCE.md records where the samples came from.

REFINED 2026-09-11. It is a toggle, available in any of the "in one position" readings of the fretboard view, not a mode of its own. There should be several examples per style rather than one. The notes a part may use follow the reading it is shown in: the chords reading gives chord tones, the pentatonic reading pentatonic notes, the scale reading scale notes. And for the pentatonic and scale readings there should be a choice between staying in the key's own scale for the whole progression and following the chord scale through each change.

RESOLVED 2026-09-11, in two rounds of questions:
- Source: a written skeleton per part with its fill bars drawn from a small per-style set. What you are working on stays put for the whole session; nothing re-rolls behind your back. Two buttons move it: one steps to the next example, one re-rolls the fills of the one you are on.
- Presentation: all three. Lit on the neck in time, written out as tab under the chart, and played along with the backing.
- Scale choice: NOT the existing Parallel / Key mode toggle, which is about how the neck is labelled. This is whether the part stays on the I scale for the whole progression or moves with the chords. When it does move, it uses whatever the neck is already showing - the notes you can see lit are the notes it plays.
- Readings: all four of Chords, Triads, Pentatonic and Scales, in their in-one-position readings.
- Parts belong to a FEEL, not a style: Jump blues gets straight-eighth parts and Shuffle swung ones. That is sixteen feels to write for.
- Two-bar phrases, call and answer: a figure then its answer or fill, looping through the progression regardless of where the chords change.

THE MODEL THIS IMPLIES (mine, not asked for, so worth checking). A part is written once per feel as rhythm plus scale degrees, and the reading decides which notes it may use: the chords reading snaps every note to a chord tone, pentatonic to the pentatonic five, scales to the whole scale, triads to the grip on the string set. Written per reading instead would be sixteen feels times four readings times several examples, which is hundreds of hand-written parts; written once and snapped, it is sixteen times a few. A degree that cannot be snapped without moving more than a tone is dropped rather than forced, so a sparse reading gives a sparser part rather than a wrong one.

PROGRESS 2026-09-11. The machinery is built end to end and the four blues feels have two parts each: parts.js holds the library and the realisation (palette per reading, snap within a tone downward-first, placement on the nearest note in the window climbing from the lowest root on the bottom three strings); the neck exposes positionView() and lightSounding(); the practice tab has the Part toggle, the part arrows, New fills and the Follow chords / Stay on the I choice in the position toolbar, draws the tab under the chart with tab.js, sounds the part on the recorded guitar from the style scheduler, lights the neck and the tab from the same animation frame that moves the chart, and carries it all in the link as p=. Still to do: parts for the other twelve feels (Rock x4, Jazz x3, Pop x3, Funk x3), once the blues ones have been heard and judged worth having. Test: every part on its feel's grid, and every realisation inside the window and the reading's notes over four readings, twelve keys and three positions - 51,840 notes.

STRUMS 2026-09-11. Both blues parts per feel rewritten as rhythm guitar with fills rather than lead lines: a new kind of note in parts.js, s(at, dur, vel), realised as the chord's CAGED grip inside the window - every string that sits in it, three at the least - swept low to high 16ms a string. Measured against the band: a strum bar adds 3.1 dB, a fill bar 3.5 dB, so the two halves sit level with each other.

summary: A toggle above the chord chart to switch between the chart and the tab/part view, with the part settings in the part view
detail: Asked for 2026-09-11, on first use of the suggested parts (T54). The part's controls - on/off, the arrows through the feel's parts, New fills, Follow chords / Stay on the I - currently sit in the neck's position toolbar, beside the box stepper, and the tab is drawn under the chord chart. Wanted instead: one toggle above the chart that switches the whole area between two views, the chord chart as it is now and a tab/part view, and the part's settings living inside the part view rather than in the neck's toolbar. Things to settle: whether the part view still shows the chord names (the tab already writes each bar's chord above it, so probably yes and the chart is simply the other reading); whether the toggle is remembered in the link alongside p=; what the part view shows when the neck isn't in one position or the feel has no parts (the toggle should say so rather than show an empty strip); and whether the beat line the chart draws has an equivalent in the part view, which is the playhead.
resolution: Done 2026-09-11. A Chart / Part toggle beside the key readout - outside the .ctl group, since the phone layout folds those away and a view switch has to be reachable on the screen it matters most on - switching the chart area between the chords as bars and the part view. Choosing Part is what turns the part on: a part you aren't looking at isn't one you're playing. The part's settings moved from the neck toolbar into the part view, above the tab: the arrows and the part's name, New fills, a volume slider with a mute (in place of the Sound / Silent pair, asked for the same day), and Follow chords / Stay on the I. The tab keeps naming each bar's chord, so the part view is a reading of the same bars rather than something else. When there is no part to show the view says why - Simple has no feel, the feel has no parts yet, the neck isn't in one position, the reading offers no notes - instead of an empty strip. Rides in the link as before (p=, now with .v<volume> and .m when they aren't the default). One thing the toggle turned up: a link opens before the neck has worked out its position, and the part view sat on 'switch to one position' while looking at one, because the window wasn't a reason to look again; whether a part is available is now part of what triggers a rebuild, with a test that reproduces the state through a progression of diminished chords, which the box readings skip. The two toggles asked for since - its own line (T57) and two-row wrapping (T56) - are rows of their own.

summary: Let the tab wrap to two lines on desktop and iPad, and scroll vertically rather than sideways
detail: Asked for 2026-09-11. The part's tab is one long strip that scrolls sideways a bar at a time (B46-B48 made it so, because a wrapped tab had no way to keep the current bar in view). Wanted on wider screens: the strip wraps to two rows instead, and the container scrolls vertically to keep the row being played in view. tab.js already knows how to wrap - measure() breaks rows at bar lines for a given width, and drawPartTab passes an enormous width to defeat that - so this is mostly choosing the width by viewport (one row on a phone, two rows from about 760px up), giving the container a height of about one row, and scrolling it to the current row's top instead of the current bar's left. playheadPos already returns the row top. Things to settle: whether two rows means half the bars each, or as many as fit; and what a twelve-bar blues does on an iPad, where two rows of six is natural and two rows of four plus four is not.
added: Done 2026-09-11. drawPartTab measures the tab's container (shown first: hidden, it measured as nothing and every screen counted as a phone) and, at 700px or more, builds the tab to that width so GT.tab wraps it; the container is held to two rows tall (overflow-y) and showPartBar scrolls it to the pair of rows the bar is on, so the page turns when the bottom row runs out. Under 700px it is the strip as before. A debounced resize redraws when the width changes. Verified at 1100px: three bars a row, page turned to the second pair at bar 6; at 600px the strip, and back again on resize.

summary: Move the Chart / Part toggle out of the key-and-progression line onto its own line
detail: Asked for 2026-09-11. T55 put the toggle beside the key readout in the chart head, outside the .ctl group so the phone layout keeps it. It crowds that line. Wanted: its own line, between the chart head and the chart itself, which also gives it room to say more than two words if that ever helps - the part's name, say, when the part view is showing.
added: Done 2026-09-11. #chartViewGroup moved out of the key-and-progression line into its own .chart-view-row under it, so it is there at every width instead of hiding with the controls under 700px.

summary: Show the Nashville number beside each chord name in the tab
detail: Asked for 2026-09-11. The tab writes each bar's chord above it (tab.js draws bar.chord); the chart underneath already knows the numeral for every chord (numeralFor, and the chart prints it under each name). Wanted: the numeral beside the name in the tab too - "A  I", "D  IV" - so the tab reads the way the chart does. drawPartTab builds the bars it hands tab.js, so this is adding the numeral there and giving tab.js a second line of text or a suffix to draw; the genre examples' tab, which has no key, should keep working with none.
added: Done 2026-09-11. GT.tab.build takes a numeral per bar and draws it after the name, quieter (.tab-numeral); practice passes chord.numeral, the genre examples pass none.

summary: Name a chord in the tab only where it changes, not over every bar it lasts
detail: Asked for 2026-09-11. drawPartTab names every bar's chord above it, so a chord held for four bars reads A A A A. A chart names it once and leaves the rest blank, and the tab should read the same way: the name where the chord arrives, nothing over the bars it carries through. tab.js draws whatever bar.chord it's given, so the change is in drawPartTab - pass the name for a bar only when it differs from the bar before. The genre examples' tab has the same habit and would take the same fix if it were made in tab.js instead; worth deciding which.
added: Done 2026-09-11. drawPartTab leaves the name and numeral off bars barCells() marks held, so a chord is named where it arrives. Every name carries data-bar, and the follower lights the nearest name at or before the bar being played (B50 records what indexing the names by bar did instead).

summary: Strums that are not always the whole grip: low strings, high strings, partial chords, as the style wants
detail: Asked for 2026-09-11. A strum in parts.js (s(at, dur, vel)) is realised as every string of the chord's CAGED grip that sits in the window. Real rhythm playing rarely hits all six every time: a shuffle leans on the low two or three strings, a jump comp stabs the top three or four, a funk chop is the top strings muted, a slow blues might hit the bass note on one and the rest on the and. Wanted: a strum can say which part of the grip it wants - something like s(at, dur, vel, 'low') / 'high' / 'top3' / 'bass' - and the parts use a mix of them as suits the feel. gripIn already returns the grip's cells with string numbers, so the selection is a filter on those; the test that holds a strum to three strings or more would need to allow a 'bass' strum of one or two. Worth deciding whether the voicing choice is per-note in the written part (explicit, more to write) or a per-feel default with per-note overrides (less to write, most bars alike).
added: Done 2026-09-11. s(at, dur, vel, voicing) in parts.js: 'full' (default), 'low' (bottom three strings of the grip), 'high' (top three), 'bass' (the lowest root, or the 5th when the window cut the root off, or the lowest note). strumCells() does the choosing; each blues part now uses the mix its idiom wants - Shuffle comp low, the stabs and jump comps high, Train chug alternating bass/high, Answering the bass root-then-top. Tests: the count per strum matches the voicing, the bass note is root or 5th, and low/high/bass are checked directly against the full grip in every key and window. Also, at the same time (asked for mid-task): each figure has two variants the phrases take in turn, so a chord held for bars isn't the same bar over and over; a test holds six bars on one chord to that and to coming out the same twice.

summary: A second volume slider, for the band
detail: Asked for 2026-09-11. The part view has a volume slider with a mute for the suggested part (partVolume, partMute). Wanted: a second slider alongside it for the band - the comp, bass and drums the style plays - so the part can be brought up against the band or the band pulled down under it. Where the band's level goes today: the style scheduler passes its own velocities to audio.playPluck/playPiano/playBass and the drums; one gain the band's voices share, before the limiter, is the simplest place for it (the part's level scales velocity per note, which would also do). Same shape as the part's control - icon that mutes, range 0-100 - and worth deciding whether it lives in the part view only or in the transport footer where the tempo is, since the band plays in the chart view too.
added: Done 2026-09-11. audio.js: every band bus (comp+tone, hi-hat, bass, drums, the genre guitar and the shared room) meets at bandGain before the limiter; the part plays on its own bus with its own copy of the tone filter and the room, playPluck(..., 'part'), so the band's level leaves the part alone (measured: part-bus RMS unchanged with the band at 0). setBandLevel()/bandLevel(); the slider and mute sit beside the part's, labelled Part / Band; the link carries it as b=<vol>[.m] on its own since the band plays in both views. Test: slider, mute, link round trip, slider unmutes.

summary: The "Controls" hide/show button in the footer at every width, desktop included
detail: Asked for 2026-09-11. The transport footer's #controlsToggle button ('Controls', aria-pressed) shows or hides the controls on the neck, and it carries .phone-only, so a desktop-width window never sees it - the controls are always out there. Wanted: offer it at every width, so a wide screen can be tidied down to the neck and the chart or part. Drop the class, check the footer has room for it beside 'Set up' and the collapse chevron at every width, and that what it hides on a desktop is the same set of controls it hides on a phone (or decide what a desktop should keep).
added: Done 2026-09-11. The Controls button lost its phone-only class (and the class itself went, nothing else used it). stage.js already decided the default by width/orientation and honoured a hand press at any width, so nothing else changed. Verified at 1200px: the button in the footer, five .ctl blocks to none on press.

summary: In the triads reading, the chord hits use only the notes of the triad shown - no sevenths, no CAGED grip
detail: Asked for 2026-09-11. palette() already keeps single notes to root, 3rd and 5th when the reading is triads3, but a strum goes through gripIn(), which takes the CAGED grip (with its 7th, when the chord has one) whichever reading is on - so in Triads the fills stay on the triad and the chord hits do not. Wanted: in Triads a strum is the triad the neck is showing - the three-string grip on the selected string set, in the window - and nothing else. gripIn would take the reading (and the string set the neck has chosen; see the triads view for where that lives) and return those three cells; the test that holds a strum to three or more chord tones passes as is, since a triad is three. Worth checking the 3rd on top / root on top voicings the triads view can show are honoured too, and that T60 (partial strums) leaves a triad whole, since there is nothing to leave out.
added: Done 2026-09-11. triadIn() in parts.js: the close triad of root/3rd/5th on the neck's string set (positionView().stringSet, new) that sits wholly in the window, lowest first; strumCells() uses it for every strum in the triads reading, 'bass' being its lowest note. Test: in triads3 every strummed note is a triad tone on strings 0-2 and each strum is three notes (or one). Sabotage-checked: with the grip restored, 'strums string 4, off the e-B-G set'.

summary: In the two-row tab, keep the row being played on top so the next row is the one in view
detail: Asked for 2026-09-11. The wrapped tab (T56) shows two rows and turns the page a pair at a time: bars on the bottom row play with the row already played above them and the next row out of sight. Wanted: scroll a row at a time so the bar being played is always on the top row and the row below is what comes next. showPartBar in practice.js sets scrollTop to floor(row/2)*2*rowSpan; make it row*rowSpan. The last row has nothing under it - either let the tab scroll to leave it on top with empty space below, or accept the final row on the bottom; decide, and keep the loop-around (the first row on top again) smooth.
